item1_text: Example Example: Mary’s LDP was September 25, 2020 (w/c 2257). Her I of E is in w/c 2257, she submitted her EI application on September 26, 2020, and her BPC will be September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258). There are 3 contentious ROEs on Mary’s file: ROE 1: LDP September 25, 2020 (w/c 2257). ROE 2: LDP July 17, 2020 (w/c 2247). ROE 3: LDP May 31, 2020 (w/c 2241). To determine which RFS to adjudicate, the officer subtracts 12 weeks from w/c 2257 (week of the I of E). For the example above, the formula is as follows: w/c 2257 (I of E) – 12 = w/c 2245. This determines a 12-week period falling before the Sunday of the I of E that encompasses the weeks from w/c 2245 to w/c 2256. The officer follows normal procedures and adjudicates ROE 1, which is the most recent ROE in the QP, and ROE 2, as it falls between w/c 2245 and w/c 2256, the 12-week period. The officer allows any contentious RFS that occurs before the 12-week period. ROE 3 is before the 12-week period, so the officer allows the RFS by following the steps of Adjudication not required — Reason for separation (RFS) beyond 12 weeks . item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: Peter’s LDP was September 28, 2021 (w/c 2310) with 2 employers. Three periods of employment are provided on his EI application. Peter declared Employer 1 as his last employer and the RFS is shortage of work. In the Other Employers section of the application, Peter declared Employer 2 and the RFS is voluntary leaving. He also declared Employer 3 and the RFS is dismissal. The interruption of earnings (I of E) is in w/c 2310, and he applied for benefits on September 29, 2021. His BPC is September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310). There are 2 contentious ROEs on Peter’s file: Employer 1: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is A . Employer 2: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is E . Employer 3: The LDP is May 19, 2021 (w/c 2291). The RFS is M . Employer 1 and Employer 2 have the same LDP. The RFS with Employer 1 is non-contentious, so adjudication is not required for Employer 2. ACP automatically resolves the RFS for Employer 2 and creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . The RFS with Employer 3 is contentious and is in the QP. However, because it is not the last employer in the QP, adjudication is not required. ACP creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . All ROEs are included in the calculation of the claim.

item1_text: Example Example: Mary’s LDP was September 25, 2020 (w/c 2257). Her I of E is in w/c 2257, she submitted her application for benefits on September 26, 2020, and her BPC will be September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258). To determine which RFS to adjudicate, the officer subtracts 12 weeks from w/c 2257 (week of the I of E). For the example above, the formula is as follows: w/c 2257 (I of E) – 12 = w/c 2245. This determines a 12-week period falling before the Sunday of the I of E that encompasses the weeks from w/c 2245 to w/c 2256. The officer follows normal procedures and adjudicates ROE 1, which is the most recent ROE in the QP, and ROE 2, as it falls between w/c 2245 and w/c 2256, the 12-week period. The officer allows any contentious RFS that occurs before the 12-week period. ROE 3 is before the 12-week period, so the officer allows the RFS by following the steps of Adjudication not required — Reason for separation (RFS) beyond 12 weeks . item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: Peter’s LDP was September 28, 2021 (w/c 2310) with 2 employers. Three periods of employment are provided on his EI application. Peter declared Employer 1 as his last employer and the RFS is shortage of work. In the Other Employers section of the application, Peter declared Employer 2 and the RFS is dismissal. He also declared Employer 3 and the RFS is voluntary leaving. The interruption of earnings (I of E) is in w/c 2310, and he applied for benefits on September 29, 2021. His BPC is September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310). There are 2 contentious ROEs on Peter’s file: Employer 1: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is A . Employer 2: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is M . Employer 3: The LDP is May 19, 2021 (w/c 2291). The RFS is E . Employer 1 and Employer 2 have the same LDP. The RFS with Employer 1 is non-contentious, so adjudication is not required for Employer 2. ACP automatically resolves the RFS for Employer 2 and creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . The RFS with Employer 3 is contentious and is in the QP. However, because it is not the last employer in the QP, adjudication is not required. ACP creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . All ROEs are included in the calculation of the claim.

This error can also occur when an employer issues a subsequent ROE using the same first day worked as a previous ROE. When this happens, the subsequent ROE may contain hours and earnings already included on the previous ROE, which may lead to incorrect benefit entitlement. The first day worked on the subsequent ROE must be corrected to indicate the first day worked since the previous ROE was issued. The officer must also ensure hours and earnings from the previous ROE are not included in the subsequent ROE. When this situation occurs and is confirmed with the employer, the dates indicated on the ROEs are correct.

Peter declared Employer 1 as his last employer and the RFS is shortage of work. In the Other Employers section of the application, Peter declared Employer 2 and the RFS is dismissal. He also declared Employer 3 and the RFS is voluntary leaving. The interruption of earnings (I of E) is in w/c 2310, and he applied for benefits on September 29, 2021. His BPC is September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310). There are 2 contentious ROEs on Peter’s file: Employer 1: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is A . Employer 2: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is M . Employer 3: The LDP is May 19, 2021 (w/c 2291). The RFS is E . Employer 1 and Employer 2 have the same LDP. The RFS with Employer 1 is non-contentious, so adjudication is not required for Employer 2. ACP automatically resolves the RFS for Employer 2 and creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . The RFS with Employer 3 is contentious and is in the QP. However, because it is not the last employer in the QP, adjudication is not required. ACP creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . All ROEs are included in the calculation of the claim.

item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: Peter’s LDP was September 28, 2021 (w/c 2310) with 2 employers. Three periods of employment are provided on his EI application. Peter declared Employer 1 as his last employer and the RFS is shortage of work. In the Other Employers section of the application, Peter declared Employer 2 and the RFS is leave of absence. He also declared Employer 3 and the RFS is voluntary leaving. The interruption of earnings (I of E) is in w/c 2310, and he applied for benefits on September 29, 2021. His BPC is September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310). There are 2 contentious ROEs on Peter’s file: Employer 1: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is A . Employer 2: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is N . Employer 3: The LDP is May 19, 2021 (w/c 2291). The RFS is E . Employer 1 and Employer 2 have the same LDP. The RFS with Employer 1 is non-contentious, so adjudication is not required for Employer 2. ACP automatically resolves the RFS for Employer 2 and creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . The RFS with Employer 3 is contentious and is in the QP. However, because it is not the last employer in the QP, adjudication is not required. ACP creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . All ROEs are included in the calculation of the claim.

ROE 2 General Motors — first day worked: August 1, 2022.LDW: September 15, 2022. RFS: P - Parental. The client takes a leave of absence from his employment with Costco on June 12, 2022. While on leave, the client begins work for a new employer, General Motors, on August 1, 2022. The client stops working for General Motors to take parental leave. The ROE indicates that the RFS is P - Parental and the LDW is September 15, 2022. The client requests a renewal for special benefits from the date that he stopped working for General Motors (September 15, 2022). The client meets the entitlement requirements for special benefits so the client’s leave of absence from Costco can be deferred. The officer manually imposes an indefinite 43 - Leave from employment without just cause disentitlement (D43) from the date the leave began (June 12, 2022). This prevents the payment of regular benefits from the BPC or date of renewal.

Examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1 The client left a permanent job offering 35 working hours per week for another permanent job offering 35 working hours per week or more. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last for 20 weeks for another temporary full-time job that was expected to last 20 weeks or more. Examples of situations that must be adjudicated at Level 2 The client left a full-time permanent job for a permanent job that is seasonal or part-time. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last a year for a new permanent part-time job. The client left a full-time permanent job for a new full-time job, despite knowing that this new employment would be of short duration.

Peter declared Employer 1 as his last employer and the RFS is shortage of work. In the Other Employers section of the application, Peter declared Employer 2 and the RFS is Voluntary leaving. He also declared Employer 3 and the RFS is dismissal. The interruption of earnings (I of E) is in w/c 2310, and he applied for benefits on September 29, 2021. His BPC is September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310). There are 2 contentious ROEs on Peter’s file: Employer 1: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is A . Employer 2: The LDP is September 28, 2021 (w/c 2309). The RFS is E . Employer 3: The LDP is May 19, 2021 (w/c 2291). The RFS is M . Employer 1 and Employer 2 have the same LDP. The RFS with Employer 1 is a non-contentious, so adjudication is not required for Employer 2. ACP automatically resolves the RFS for Employer 2 and creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . The RFS with Employer 3 is a contentious and is in the QP. However, because it is not the last employer in the QP, adjudication is not required. ACP creates a ROD that shows Adjudication not required . All ROEs are included in the calculation of the claim.

Although the PRP “Reduction Ended” status code has a “Received Date” of March 04, because this is a new allocation, the agent inputs the allocation information and applies the status (“Reduction Ended”) from the Sunday of the first full week of January. In this exceptional case, the status code change cannot go back to the beginning of the allocation because we know that the employer had a reduction in 2018 (as of January 26, 2019) . The 100% earnings deduction rule would be maintained from December 02, 2018 to January 05, 2019, and the 50% earnings deduction rule would apply from January 06, 2019 to the end of the allocation (March 15, 2019). An overpayment would result because, originally, the benefit payments would have generated full EI payments. The new allocation information would create the overpayment; no additional overpayment is created as a result of the PRP status change.

Although the PRP “Reduction Ended” status code has a “Received Date” of March 04, because this is a new allocation, the agent inputs the allocation information and applies the status (“Reduction Ended”) from the Sunday of the first full week of January. In this exceptional case, the status code change cannot go back to the beginning of the allocation because we know that the employer had a reduction in 2018 (as of January 26, 2019) . The 100% earnings deduction rule would be maintained from December 02, 2018 to January 05, 2019, and the 50% earnings deduction rule would apply from January 06, 2019 to the end of the allocation (March 15, 2019). An overpayment would result because, originally, the benefit payments would have generated full EI payments. The new allocation information would create the overpayment; no additional overpayment is created as a result of the PRP status change.

item1_text: Example Example: Francis establishes a BP for regular benefits with 525 hours. He serves the waiting period (WP) and 3 weeks of definite disqualification before he returns to work. He works 400 hours and then stops working due to illness. Francis is not entitled to sickness benefits on the established BP since he is minor attached. If he requests a cancellation of the established BP, the hours used to establish the minor-attached BP can be combined with the 400 hours worked after that BP was established. This would allow Francis to establish a new, major-attached BP, as long as the hours fall within the new QP. If at least 200 of the 525 hours worked fall within the QP, Francis would now be major attached and qualify for sickness benefits.

Although the PRP “Reduction Ended” status code has a “Received Date” of March 04, because this is a new allocation, the agent inputs the allocation information and applies the status (“Reduction Ended”) from the start date of the allocation (February 04). The 50% earnings deduction rule would apply and an overpayment would result because, originally, the benefit payments would have generated full EI payments. Although the PRP “Reduction Ended” status code has a “Received Date” of March 04, in the absence of the effective date of the PRP status change, the PRP status (“Reduction Ended”) is applied from the start date of the allocation (Jan 13) so as to ensure the claimant receives all benefits they may be entitled to (and prevent the claimant having to submit a Request for Reconsideration to recover any potential underpayment). item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend a bona fide job interview. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will not be returning to Canada until May 20, 2016. To determine the 7-day allowable period, the agent must exclude the day of departure (May 9, 2016) and count 7 consecutive days beginning with May 10, 2016. Since the client is not returning to Canada until a later date, a 13 - Outside Canada disentitlement (D13) is imposed effective May 17, 2016 up to and including May 19, 2016, the day before the date of return. item1_text: Callout Hello, We are writing to inform you about your Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) paid by Service Canada through the Employment Insurance (EI) program. We have determined that your CERB will end soon. These benefits end when the maximum of $14,000 over 28 weeks has been paid, or on October 3, 2020, whichever comes first. Once your CERB ends, we will automatically review your file and start a new claim for EI regular benefits if you qualify. Do not file a new application for EI benefits. Filing a new application may delay the processing of your claim. We need your record(s) of employment (ROE) as soon as possible to determine if you qualify for EI benefits and to determine how much you will receive. You can check if your ROE(s) has been submitted and is accurate in your My Service Canada Account (MSCA). If your employer has not submitted your ROE, please remind them to do so as soon as possible. If we do not receive your ROE, it may delay the processing of your claim. Once you receive your last CERB payment, continue completing reports while we assess your claim and determine if you qualify for EI regular benefits. Please note that the EI program is changing, so that EI is easier to access and more people will qualify. Service Canada will communicate more details in the coming weeks. Follow Canada.ca to obtain the latest information. Yours sincerely,

item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend the funeral of an immediate family member. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will not be returning to Canada until May 20, 2016. To determine the 7-day allowable period, the officer must exclude the day of departure (May 9, 2016) and count 7 consecutive days beginning with May 10, 2016. The 7-day allowable period will end as of May 16, 2016. A D59 is imposed from May 9, 2016 (the day of departure) to May 16, 2016 (the allowable period of 7 days following the day of departure). Since the client is not returning to Canada until a later date, a D13 is imposed effective May 17, 2016 up to and including May 19, 2016, the day before the return date.
item2_text: Example 2 Example 2: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend the funeral of an immediate family member. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will be returning to Canada on May 17, 2016 (the 8th day). A D59 is imposed from May 9, 2016 (the day of departure) to May 16, 2016 (the allowable period of 7 days following the day of departure). Since the client is returning to Canada on the 8th day, a D13 is not imposed for being out of Canada on that day.

item1_text: Callout Communication #1 - Service Canada CERB claimants automatically enrolled to EI Hello, We are writing to inform you about your Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) paid by Service Canada through the Employment Insurance (EI) program. Once your CERB ends, we will automatically review your file and start a new claim for EI regular benefits if you qualify. Do not file a new application for EI benefits. Filing a new application may delay the processing of your claim. We need your record(s) of employment (ROE) as soon as possible to determine if you qualify for EI benefits and to determine how much you will receive. You can check if your ROE(s) has been submitted and is accurate in your My Service Canada Account (MSCA). If your employer has not submitted your ROE, please remind them to do so as soon as possible. If we do not receive your ROE, it may delay the processing of your claim. Once you receive your last CERB payment, continue completing reports while we assess your claim and determine if you qualify for EI regular benefits. Please note that the EI program is changing in August, so that EI is easier to access and more people will qualify. Service Canada will communicate more details in the coming weeks. Follow Canada.ca to obtain the latest information. Yours sincerely,

item1_text: Note Note: Some employers may have policies that allow employees to begin their maternity leave a fixed number of weeks before the expected DOB (e.g. in British Columbia, provincial employees can start maternity leave 6 weeks before their expected due date). In such situations, the officer does not advise the employee to apply for sickness benefits before maternity benefits, unless her particular circumstances require it. If the officer incorrectly advises the client, the following problems may occur: When a client receives sickness benefits before maternity benefits, the EI program may become the first payer. Employers registered with the Premium Reduction Program (PRP) must be the first payer to meet the program’s requirements. An employee claiming sickness benefits before maternity benefits can therefore jeopardize her employer’s entitlement to the PRP. There may be an impact on the payment of maternity or parental supplementary unemployment benefits (SUB): if a client receives sickness benefits before maternity benefits, she may lose her entitlement to SUB payments for the WP; the SUB may be payable for a definite period after ceasing work because that period is deemed the maternity or parental leave period. After the definite period has expired, the client may be able to obtain approval from her employer for an extended leave. However, an extended leave would fall outside the period for which the SUB is payable. Therefore, the client may be denied her full SUB entitlement, or the employer may be compelled to pay the SUB into the period of extended leave. For these reasons, it is important that a client apply for the appropriate benefit type (BT) based on her circumstances.

Passage 1 indicates a 'Reduction' status leading to an overpayment, while Passage 2 indicates a 'Reduction Ended' status leading to an underpayment. item1_text: Callout (A) PRP status = Reduction (ER has PRP history) BPC = Feb 03, 2019 (w/c 2172) Benefit Type = Sickness No WLI or PSL allocation at time of BPC Claimant calls on March 18, 2019 to advise EI of a new WLI allocation; WLI allocation has weekly amount = $750, a start date of Feb 04, 2019 (w/c 2172), and an end date of May 18, 2019 (w/c 2186) In FTS: 2019 PRP status code = Reduction, Received date = Jan 26, 2019 2018 PRP status code = Reduction, Received date = Jan 26, 2019 Result: At the time the claimant reports the new allocation information, the PRP status code in FTS is “Reduction”. The agent inputs the allocation information and applies the status (“Reduction”) from the start date of the allocation. The 100% earnings deduction rule would apply and an overpayment would result because, originally, the benefit payments would have generated full EI payments. The new allocation information would create the overpayment; no additional overpayment is created as a result of the PRP status.
item2_text: Callout (A) PRP status = “Reduction” to “Reduction Ended” (ER has PRP history) BPC = Jan 13, 2019 (w/c 2169) Benefit Type = Sickness WLI allocation at BPC = STRT-WK: Jan 13 (w/c 2169), END-WK: indefinite (w/c 9999), WK-AMT: $750 Claimant calls on April 02, 2019 to advise EI of the end date (March 29, 2019) of the WLI allocation In FTS: 2019 PRP status code = Reduction Ended, Received date = March 04, 2019 2019 PRP status code = Reduction, Received date = Jan 26, 2019 2018 PRP status code = Reduction, Received Date = Jan 26, 2019 Result: At the time the claimant reports a change to the WLI allocation, the PRP status code in FTS is “Reduction Ended”. Although the PRP “Reduction Ended” status code has a “Received Date” of March 04, in the absence of the effective date of the PRP status change, the PRP status (“Reduction Ended”) is applied from the start date of the allocation (Jan 13) so as to ensure the claimant receives all benefits they may be entitled to (and prevent the claimant having to submit a Request for Reconsideration to recover any potential underpayment). The 50% earnings deduction rule would apply to the entire allocation period (January 13, 2019 to March 29, 2019), with an underpayment created because, originally, the benefit payments for this period would have generated no EI payments.

The agent inputs the allocation information and applies the status (“Reduction”) from the start date of the allocation. Since there are only 37 remaining weeks of benefits and the parents cannot decide how to share the benefits, a decision is made for them. item1_text: Info Example 1 On December 10, 2017, a client who wants to care for her critically ill or injured child establishes a claim for FCB for children. She requests 35 weeks of benefits. After serving the waiting period (WP), the client receives 9 weeks of benefits. On February 18, 2018, the other parent establishes a claim for FCB and requests 20 weeks of benefits. As there are only 26 weeks of benefits left and the clients cannot decide who will get them, the Level 2 officer decides for them. The number of unpaid weeks can be equally divided between the clients. They both receive 13 weeks of benefits. The client’s total of FCB weeks paid is 22 and the other family member’s is 13, for a total of 35 weeks of FCB for children paid.
item2_text: Info Example 3 On December 17, 2017, a client who wants to care for her critically ill or injured child establishes a claim for FCB for children. The client request 35 weeks of benefits and receives 34. On August 23, 2018, the child’s grandmother establishes a claim to care for the critically ill or injured child. She requests 35 weeks of benefits. As there is only one week of benefits remaining to be paid, the officer assigns it to the client who submitted a claim for benefits first. Therefore, the client receives 35 weeks of benefits and the grandmother does not receive any.

final_analysis: Both passages describe scenarios involving parental benefits claims from two parents, but they present mutually incompatible claims regarding the distribution of benefits. In Passage 1, the first parent ends up with a total of 35 weeks and the second parent with 5 weeks, while in Passage 2, the first parent ends up with 33 weeks and the second parent with 7 weeks. item1_text: Example 3 Example 3: A client files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The other parent requests 5 weeks of standard parental benefits. After having received the 5 weeks, the other parent requests an additional 5 weeks. The first parent has already received 34 weeks. Since there is only 1 remaining week of benefits and the parents cannot decide how to share the benefits, a decision is made for them. The remaining week is assigned to the parent who first applied for parental benefits. The first parent’s total entitlement is 35 weeks (34 already paid + 1 remaining week) and the other parent’s is 5, for a combined total of 40 weeks of standard parental benefits. No additional weeks of benefits are payable to the other parent.
item2_text: Example Example: The first parent files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The client has already been paid 25 weeks of benefits when the other parent requests 25 weeks of benefits. The parental entitlement is reviewed 10 weeks later and it is determined that the first parent has now received 35 weeks of benefits and the other parent has received 10 weeks. This exceeds the maximum 40 weeks that can be shared between parents. The parents cannot agree on how to revise the entitlement weeks, so the officer considers the claims at the date when the other parent applied for benefits. At the date of the other parent’s application, 25 weeks had been paid to the first parent and there were 15 remaining to be paid. The officer assigns the 15 remaining weeks equally, starting with the first parent who applied. The first parent will be entitled to a total of 33 weeks and the other parent will be entitled to a total of 7 weeks. The officer revises the entitlement and creates an OP on both claims.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the conditions for adjudicating voluntary leaving to accept other employment at Level 1, but they present conflicting criteria regarding the timing of the new employment in relation to the last day worked (LDW) from the previous employment. Passage 1 states that the new employment must start within 4 weeks of the LDW, while Passage 2 specifies a maximum of a 4-day gap. Additionally, Passage 1 includes examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1, which are not present in Passage 2, leading to further discrepancies in the interpretation of the conditions.
item1_text: Callout Voluntary leaving to accept other employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new employment started within 4 weeks of the LDW of the previous employment; and the BPC or renewal week is after the week the new employment started; and the new employment was supposed to be a permanent position; or if the new job was temporary, it was to last longer than the job the client quit; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1 The client left a permanent job offering 35 working hours per week for another permanent job offering 35 working hours per week or more. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last for 20 weeks for another temporary full-time job that was expected to last 20 weeks or more. Examples of situations that must be adjudicated at Level 2 The client left a full-time permanent job for a permanent job that is seasonal or part-time. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last a year for a new permanent part-time job. The client left a full-time permanent job for a new full-time job, despite knowing that this new employment would be of short duration.
item2_text: Callout Voluntary leaving to accept other employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new employment was supposed to be permanent; and there was no more than a 4-day gap between the first day worked with the new employment and the LDW from the previous employment; or the first day worked with the new employment started before the LDW at the previous employment; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Voluntary leaving temporary employment to accept other temporary employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new temporary employment was supposed to last longer than the previous temporary employment; and there was no more than a 4-day gap between the first day worked with the new employment and the LDW from the previous employment; or the first day worked with the new employment started before the LDW from the previous employment; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Note: Temporary employment is defined as a seasonal, contract, or term employment, and has an end date. Permanent employment is defined as a lasting employment, or an employment that is intended to last or to remain unchanged indefinitely. It has no end date. Voluntary leaving employment to continue working in full-time employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the client had more than one employment at the same time and voluntarily left one of them; and the employment the client kept was full-time and the client was not expecting it to end. Note: On a continuing claim, all voluntary leaving for other employment must be adjudicated at Level 2, except in the situations described above.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss conditions for voluntary leaving to accept new employment, but they present conflicting criteria regarding the timing and nature of the new employment. Passage 1 requires the new employment to start within 2 weeks and can be temporary, while Passage 2 allows for a start within 4 weeks and specifies that the new job should ideally be permanent or, if temporary, must last longer than the previous job. This creates mutually incompatible claims regarding the conditions for adjudication.
item1_text: Callout Voluntary leaving when there is a reasonable assurance of other temporary employment — Conditions to adjudicate the Issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the client had a genuine employment offer that was scheduled to start within 2 weeks of the LDW of the previous employment. Confirmation from the prospective employer is required; and the client did not start the new employment because the offer was withdrawn or cancelled for reasons unrelated to the client or the client’s actions. Confirmation from the prospective employer is required; and the client was unable to withdraw the resignation from the previous employment and was unable to return to it; and the client quit one temporary employment for another temporary employment; and the new temporary employment was supposed to last the same amount of time or longer than the previous temporary employment; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment would have been equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS.
item2_text: Callout Voluntary leaving to accept other employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new employment started within 4 weeks of the LDW of the previous employment; and the BPC or renewal week is after the week the new employment started; and the new employment was supposed to be a permanent position; or if the new job was temporary, it was to last longer than the job the client quit; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1 The client left a permanent job offering 35 working hours per week for another job offering 35 working hours per week or more. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last for 20 weeks for another temporary full-time job that was expected to last 20 weeks or more. Examples of situations that must be adjudicated at Level 2 The client left a full-time permanent job for a permanent job that is seasonal or part-time. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last a year for a new permanent part-time job. The client left a full-time permanent job for a new full-time temporary job, despite knowing that this new employment would be of short duration.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss claimants who are full-time students and their work availability while studying. However, they present conflicting information regarding the claimants' willingness to work during the week. Passage 1 indicates that the claimant is unwilling to work during the week unless their studies allow it, while Passage 2 states that the claimant is prepared to work at any time except when in class. This fundamental difference in their availability creates a conflict in the assessment of their circumstances.
item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: BPC: September 3, 2023 (w/c 2411) The claimant is a full-time university student (third session started on September 5, 2023; the claimant started their program in September 2022). The claimant previously worked approximately 10 hours a week starting August 26, 2022; was laid off September 1, 2023. The claimant stated that while studying, they worked mostly during weekends. They preferred not working during the week, but they accepted an evening shift from time to time. The claimant is unwilling to abandon their classes to accept a suitable employment and is still looking to work mainly on the weekends. The claimant states they would not accept working hours during the week unless their studies allow them to (i.e. when they have fewer assignments or when the school is closed). Despite that the facts show a work history while attending school full time, all criteria to show exceptional circumstances are not met. Unlike in the Page decision, the claimant’s availability is very limited as they are not willing to accept work during the week. It can be argued that such a restricted availability unduly limits their chances to find employment. Although this claimant does not rebut the presumption of non-availability, the other 2 criteria of Faucher must be evaluated to complete the availability assessment.
item2_text: Example 2 Example 2: BPC: October 15, 2023 (w/c 2417) The claimant is a full-time college student (third session started on August 21, 2023, the claimant started their program in August 2022). The claimant worked approximately 17 hours a week starting January 5, 2023; was laid off on October 7, 2023. Their work schedule was 2 shifts during the weekend and one or 2 shifts during weekdays, mainly in the evening. The claimant stated that while studying, they were prepared to work at any time except when they were in class. The claimant would have worked up to 25 hours a week, they requested more shifts, but their employer was unable to give more hours. The claimant’s former employer confirmed and stated that the claimant requested more shifts but there was not enough work to grant the request. The claimant is unwilling to abandon their classes to accept employment but is still looking to work on a similar schedule as they had with their previous employer. The claimant says they are ready to work as many hours as are offered but admits that working more than 25 hours per week might prove difficult. The facts show a regular work history outside of class hours while attending school full time, which would be sufficient to show exceptional circumstances. Just like in the Page decision, the claimant provided a wide availability to be scheduled for shifts when they worked previously, and they are still prepared to work on a similar schedule. The number of hours during the work history is not the sole factor to be considered. It is the entirety of the claimant’s situation and intentions that must be taken into account in determining whether the claimant shows exceptional circumstances or not. Although this claimant does rebut the presumption of non-availability, the other 2 criteria of Faucher must be evaluated to complete the availability assessment.

item1_text: Info Example: A client’s expected DOB is July 1, 2019, and she had not prearranged her maternity leave with her employer. The client becomes ill in March 2019, and her doctor recommends that she take sick leave until the DOB. The officer sets up a claim for sickness benefits until the week before the expected DOB (the week of June 23 to 29, 2019). The client later reports that she gave birth on Wednesday June 5, 2019. The client is considered not otherwise available as of the week starting June 2, 2019 because she gave birth. Therefore, she cannot receive sickness benefits from June 2 to June 29, even though her doctor recommended that she take sick leave during this period. However, she could receive maternity benefits. If the client wants to receive sickness benefits during this period, a Level 2 officer adjudicates the issue.
item2_text: Example Example: The client planned and made arrangements with her employer to start her maternity leave June 3, 2019. The client becomes ill in March 2019, and her doctor recommends that she take sick leave until the delivery date. The client is not due until July 1, 2019. She is not otherwise available as of June 3 because she already made arrangements to be on maternity leave. Therefore, she cannot receive sickness benefits between June 2 and June 30, even though her doctor recommended that she take sick leave during this period. She could, however, receive maternity benefits.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the conditions for adjudicating voluntary leaving to accept other employment at Level 1, but they present conflicting criteria regarding the timing of the new employment in relation to the last day worked (LDW) from the previous employment. Passage 1 states that the new employment must start within 4 weeks of the LDW, while Passage 2 specifies a maximum of a 4-day gap. Additionally, Passage 1 includes examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1, which are not mentioned in Passage 2, leading to conflicting interpretations of the criteria.
item1_text: Callout Voluntary leaving to accept other employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new employment started within 4 weeks of the LDW of the previous employment; and the BPC or renewal week is after the week the new employment started; and the new employment was supposed to be a permanent position; or if the new job was temporary, it was to last longer than the job the client quit; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1 The client left a permanent job offering 35 working hours per week for another job offering 35 working hours per week or more. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last for 20 weeks for another temporary full-time job that was expected to last 20 weeks or more. Examples of situations that must be adjudicated at Level 2 The client left a full-time permanent job for a permanent job that is seasonal or part-time. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last a year for a new permanent part-time job. The client left a full-time permanent job for a new full-time temporary job, despite knowing that this new employment would be of short duration.
item2_text: Callout Voluntary leaving to accept other employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new employment was supposed to be permanent; and there was no more than a 4-day gap between the first day worked with the new employment and the LDW from the previous employment; or the first day worked with the new employment started before the LDW at the previous employment; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Voluntary leaving temporary employment to accept other temporary employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the new temporary employment was supposed to last longer than the previous temporary employment; and there was no more than a 4-day gap between the first day worked with the new employment and the LDW from the previous employment; or the first day worked with the new employment started before the LDW from the previous employment; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment was equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS. Note: Temporary employment is defined as a seasonal, contract, or term employment, and has an end date. Permanent employment is defined as a lasting employment, or an employment that is intended to last or to remain unchanged indefinitely. It has no end date. Voluntary leaving employment to continue working in full-time employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the client had more than one employment at the same time and voluntarily left one of them; and the employment the client kept was full-time and the client was not expecting it to end. Note: On a continuing claim, all voluntary leaving for other employment must be adjudicated at Level 2, except in the situations described above.

item1_text: Example 2 Example 2: A client files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The other parent subsequently requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits, but the first parent has already received 3 weeks. Since there are only 37 remaining weeks of benefits and the parents cannot decide how to share the benefits, a decision is made for them. The number of remaining weeks cannot be equally divided between them. The remaining weeks are divided as equally as possible and the extra week is assigned to the parent who first applied for parental benefits. The first parent’s total entitlement is 22 (3 already paid + 19 of the remaining weeks) and the other parent’s is 18, for a combined total of 40 weeks of standard parental benefits.
item2_text: Example Example: The first parent files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The client has already been paid 25 weeks of benefits when the other parent requests 25 weeks of benefits. The parental entitlement is reviewed 10 weeks later and it is determined that the first parent has now received 35 weeks of benefits and the other parent has received 10 weeks. This exceeds the maximum 40 weeks that can be shared between parents. The parents cannot agree on how to revise the entitlement weeks, so the officer considers the claims at the date when the other parent applied for benefits. At the date of the other parent’s application, 25 weeks had been paid to the first parent and there were 15 remaining to be paid. The officer assigns the 15 remaining weeks equally, starting with the first parent who applied. The first parent will be entitled to a total of 33 weeks and the other parent will be entitled to a total of 7 weeks. The officer revises the entitlement and creates an OP on both claims.

final_analysis: Both passages describe a scenario involving two parents requesting parental benefits, but they present conflicting details regarding the number of weeks already paid, the total weeks requested, and the final entitlements assigned to each parent. Passage 1 states that the first parent has received 30 weeks and the second parent 0 weeks, while Passage 2 states that the first parent has received 35 weeks and the second parent 10 weeks. item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The other parent subsequently requests 15 weeks of standard parental benefits, but the first parent has already received 30 weeks. Since there are only 10 remaining weeks of shareable benefits and the parents cannot decide how to share the benefits, a decision is made for them. The number of remaining weeks can be equally divided between them. Each parent is entitled to 5 of the remaining weeks. The first parent’s total entitlement is 35 (30 already paid + 5 of the remaining weeks) and the other parent’s is 5, for a combined total of 40 weeks of standard parental benefits.
item2_text: Example Example: The first parent files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The client has already been paid 25 weeks of benefits when the other parent requests 25 weeks of benefits. The parental entitlement is reviewed 10 weeks later and it is determined that the first parent has now received 35 weeks of benefits and the other parent has received 10 weeks. This exceeds the maximum 40 weeks that can be shared between parents. The parents cannot agree on how to revise the entitlement weeks, so the officer considers the claims at the date when the other parent applied for benefits. At the date of the other parent’s application, 25 weeks had been paid to the first parent and there were 15 remaining to be paid. The officer assigns the 15 remaining weeks equally, starting with the first parent who applied. The first parent will be entitled to a total of 33 weeks and the other parent will be entitled to a total of 7 weeks. The officer revises the entitlement and creates an OP on both claims.

item1_text: Callout Voluntary leaving when there is a reasonable assurance of other permanent employment — Conditions to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 (all conditions must be met) the client had a genuine employment offer that was scheduled to start within 2 weeks of the LDW of the previous employment. Confirmation from the prospective employer is required; and the client did not start the new employment because the offer was withdrawn or cancelled for reasons unrelated to the client or the client’s actions. Confirmation from the prospective employer required; and the client was unable to withdraw the resignation from the previous employment and unable to return to it; and the new job was supposed to be permanent; and the weekly number of hours at the new employment would have been equal to or greater than the weekly number of hours worked at the previous employment; and there are no contentious issues related to the voluntary leaving that would prevent the Level 1 officer from allowing the RFS.

Examples of situations that can be adjudicated at Level 1 The client left a permanent job offering 35 working hours per week for another job offering 35 working hours per week or more. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last for 20 weeks for another temporary full-time job that was expected to last 20 weeks or more. Examples of situations that must be adjudicated at Level 2 The client left a full-time permanent job for a permanent job that is seasonal or part-time. The client left a temporary full-time job that was expected to last a year for a new permanent part-time job. The client left a full-time permanent job for a new full-time temporary job, despite knowing that this new employment would be of short duration.

item1_text: Callout Hello, We are writing to you about the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) you received from Service Canada in 2020. Our records show that you repaid $ [XXXX.XX] of this amount in 2021. When filing your taxes, you can claim a deduction for the amount you repaid: on line 23210 of your 2021 return; on line 23200 of your 2020 return; or on both your 2020 and 2021 returns, if you want to split the deduction between the two tax returns. The amount claimed cannot be more than the total of: the amount indicated above; and the amount in box 201 of your T4A slip, if you received one. If you’re claiming the full amount on your 2021 return Enter the amount you repaid on line 23210 of your 2021 return, even if your T4E slip indicates to enter the amount on line 23200. If you repaid any other EI benefits in 2021, you can claim a deduction for that amount by entering it on line 23200 of your tax return. If you’re claiming the full amount on your 2020 return If you want to claim the amount on your 2020 return, but the Canada Revenue Agency has already issued you a notice of assessment, you will have to request a change to your tax return. For more information, visit Canada.ca/change-tax-return. You must keep this letter for six years after you file your return, as it is supporting documentation for your return. If the Canada Revenue Agency wants you to keep it for a longer period, they will let you know. The employer issues ROEs to the employees at the end of each week because they are not scheduled to work the following week. The reason for separation is shortage of work, with an expected return to work of the following week. The Employment Standards Act for the province of work indicates that 40 hours per week is considered as full-time employment. Since the employees are not working every second week and are not paid for those weeks, they request EI benefits for the week they do not work. item1_text: Note Note: Separation monies are not allocated on initial, renewal and continuing claims if one of the following conditions is met: The BPC is between March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493), and October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ). The separation monies would otherwise be allocated under EIR 36(9) to 36(11) and the first week of allocation falls within the period beginning March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493) to October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ). EIR 36(9) 36(11) The BPC is between September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258) and September 19, 2021 (w/c 2309). The renewal week is between September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258) and September 19, 2021 (w/c 2309) and allocations that were already on the initial claim being renewed in w/c 2258 or after remain even if the allocation goes beyond w/c 2258. The allocation start date is between September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258) and September 24, 2021 (w/c 2309). The separation monies are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), regardless of the BPC. The separation monies are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362) and the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361). This measure applies to all EI claim types (CTs) and to EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) claims. item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend a bona fide job interview. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will not be returning to Canada until May 20, 2016. To determine the 7-day allowable period, the agent must exclude the day of departure (May 9, 2016) and count 7 consecutive days beginning with May 10, 2016. The 7-day allowable period will end as of May 16, 2016. A D59 is imposed for the allowable period from May 9, 2016 to May 16, 2016. Since the client is not returning to Canada until a later date, a 13 - Outside Canada disentitlement (D13) is imposed effective May 17, 2016 up to and including May 19, 2016, the day before the date of return. A D3 is also imposed if the client cannot prove availability for the same period.
item2_text: Example 2 Example 2: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend the funeral of an immediate family member. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will be returning to Canada on May 17, 2016 (the 8th day). A D59 is imposed from May 9, 2016 (the day of departure) to May 16, 2016 (the allowable period of 7 days following the day of departure). Since the client is returning to Canada on the 8th day, a D13 is not imposed for being out of Canada on that day.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the BRAC provisions for tax year 2019, but they provide different calculations for the OP value. Passage 1 states the OP value is $250, while Passage 2 states it is $350, leading to mutually incompatible claims regarding the same scoped case.
item1_text: Example 1 Example 1: The client is subject to BRAC provisions for tax year 2019. In November 2019, a $400 regular benefit OP was established for tax year 2019. In December 2019, a $150 recoupment from EI benefits applied to the OP. In January 2020, a $100 recoupment from EI benefits applied to the OP. The OP value for the BRAC calculation for tax year 2019 is $250. This amount is based on the following calculation: $400 (OP established in the year benefits were paid) – $150 (OP recouped in the 2019 tax year) = $250 The $100 OP recouped after the benefit repayment year does not affect the BRAC amount.
item2_text: Example 3 Example 3: The client is subject to BRAC provisions for tax year 2019. In May 2019, a $300 regular benefit OP was established for tax year 2019. In June 2019, a $200 special benefit (sickness benefits) OP was established for tax year 2019. In July 2019, an adjustment to the regular benefit OP was processed, reducing it by $100. In January 2020, there was a $150 regular benefit OP established for tax year 2019. The OP value for the BRAC calculation for tax year 2019 is $350. The amount is based on the following calculation: $300 (regular benefit OP) – $100 (adjustment) + $150 (regular benefit OP established in 2020) = $350 The $200 special benefit OP is not subject to the BRAC provisions.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the treatment of separation monies in relation to specific time frames and conditions. However, they present conflicting claims regarding whether separation monies are considered earnings and allocated during the specified periods. Passage 1 states that separation monies are reviewed and can be allocated under certain conditions, while Passage 2 asserts that they are not considered earnings and are not allocated during the same review period. This creates a direct contradiction in the handling of separation monies.

The separation monies would otherwise be allocated under EIR 36(9) to 36(11) and the first week of allocation falls within the period beginning March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493) to October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ). The allocation start date is between September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258) and September 24, 2021 (w/c 2309). This measure applies to all EI claim types (CTs) and to EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) claims. item2_text: Note Note: A Budget 2021 measure applies to separation monies that are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361) and are paid due to a permanent separation from employment. When separation monies are reviewed during that period, they are not considered earnings and are not allocated, regardless of the BPC. If the WEPP payment includes separation monies, the officer does not allocate it. A transitional provision applies to separation monies that are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362). When the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), monies paid or payable due to a permanent separation from employment are not considered earnings and are not allocated.

The client being unable to perform the tasks required requires Level 1 adjudication, but being late requires Level 2 adjudication.

The EI ERB was not paid in the first previous period (w/c 2234 to 2235), so the officer omits those weeks. The officer reviews the previous weeks (w/c 2232 to 2233) in which there is income of $700. The total earnings amount is now $1 400. Since this total exceeds $1 000, the officer may need to impose a D47 in the 2-week period under review (w/c 2236 to 2237) to create an OP. The officer does not impose a D47 on the previous 2 weeks that were used in the total earnings in the review (w/c 2232 to 2233) because the period under review is w/cs 2236 and 2237. w/c 2238: The EI ERB was paid and the client reported no earnings. w/c 2239: The EI ERB was paid and the client reported earnings of $100. The officer reviews the 2-week period (w/c 2240 to 2241) and finds earnings of $1 100. Since this amount exceeds the $1 000 threshold, the officer may need to impose a D47 to create an OP. There is no need to review any previous weeks because the earnings have already exceeded the $1 000 threshold. Therefore, the condition under EIA 153.9(4) is not met. In summary, the officer may need to impose a D47 on w/c 2236, 2237, 2240 and 2241 as these were the 2-week periods under review, and the officer determined that the client did not meet the income loss requirements under EIA 153.9(4) for these periods (i.e. having earnings less than $1 000 in a 4-week period). The officer does not impose the D47 on all 4 weeks in which the client was not eligible to receive the EI ERB. Example 2 Claimant stops working on September 23, 2022 (w/c 2361), has a full work week earning their normal weekly earnings, and receives vacation pay and severance pay due to the complete separation. They apply for benefits and the BPC is established as of September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362). The monies on separation are considered earnings and are allocated, starting the week of September 25, 2022, due to the fact that the claimant had earned their normal weekly earnings in their last week worked. Example 3 Claimant stops working on September 9, 2022 (w/c 2359) and applies for benefits on September 27, 2022. The claimant receives vacation pay and severance pay due to separation. Although the claimant applied after September 25, 2022, the BPC is established as of September 11, 2022 (w/c 2360) and the start date of the allocation is also the week of September 11, 2022 (w/c 2360). The monies paid due to the separation are not allocated on the claim because the allocation start date is prior to September 25, 2022. Example 4 Claimant stopped working due to a permanent separation on October 9, 2020 (w/c 2259) and applied for benefits. At that time, the claimant received pay in-lieu-of notice and severance pay and the BPC was established as of October 11, 2020 (w/c 2260). The separation monies were not allocated because of the temporary measures in place at the time. The claimant calls on November 2, 2022 (w/c 2367) to advise that they recently received additional severance pay from that same employer related to the same work stoppage. The additional severance pay is not allocated against the claim because the original allocation was not applied due to the temporary measures in place at the time. Amended allocation information is treated in the same manner as the original allocation. Example 5 Claimant stops working on June 15, 2022 (w/c 2347) and receives a substantial amount of severance pay. They apply for benefits on October 3, 2022. The system established the BPC as of October 2, 2022 (w/c 2363). Although the claimant applied late and has a BPC of October 2, 2022 (w/c 2363, after the coming-into-force date), the severance pay allocation start week is the week of the lay-off (June 12, 2022 (w/c 2347). The start week of the allocation is prior to September 25, 2022 and falls under the transitional provision. Therefore, it is not considered as earnings and is not allocated. Example 6 Claimant renews their February 27, 2022 claim (BPC w/c 2332) on October 16, 2022 (w/c 2365) and advises the Commission that they received severance pay following their layoff on October 14, 2022. The severance pay will be allocated on the renewal claim as it is considered earnings as of September 25, 2022. Example 7 A claimant establishes an initial claim on February 6, 2022 (BPC w/c 2329) and collects 7 weeks of benefits. The claimant returns to work for the same employer on April 4, 2022. The claimant then experiences a subsequent complete separation from that employment on August 5, 2022 (FWW earning normal weekly earnings) and receives 12 weeks of severance pay. Thinking they were not entitled to benefits due to the severance package, the claimant only applies to renew their claim on October 17, 2022 (w/c 2365). The renewal claim is established with a renewal week of October 9, 2022 (w/c 2364) as a late renewal application can be backdated by one week. Although the renewal week is after the coming-into-force week, the start week of the potential allocation of severance pay is the week following the layoff (w/c 2355). As a result, the start week of the allocation falls under the transitional provision period, is not considered as earnings, and is not allocated against the claim.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss parental benefits for the same child, but they present conflicting details regarding the number of weeks claimed and paid. Passage 1 states that both parents applied for 40 weeks and received benefits that exceeded this maximum, while Passage 2 details a scenario where the first parent requested 35 weeks and the second parent requested 25 weeks, leading to a different distribution of weeks that also exceeds the maximum. The discrepancies in the claims and outcomes indicate a conflict.
item1_text: Example Example: The client applies for 40 weeks of standard parental benefits and the spouse applies for 40 weeks of standard parental benefits. An investigation reveals that both parents were receiving benefits for the same child and the number of weeks paid exceeds the maximum entitlement of 40 weeks.
item2_text: Example Example: The first parent files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The client has already been paid 25 weeks of benefits when the other parent requests 25 weeks of benefits. The parental entitlement is reviewed 10 weeks later and it is determined that the first parent has now received 35 weeks of benefits and the other parent has received 10 weeks. This exceeds the maximum 40 weeks that can be shared between parents. The parents cannot agree on how to revise the entitlement weeks, so the officer considers the claims at the date when the other parent applied for benefits. At the date of the other parent’s application, 25 weeks had been paid to the first parent and there were 15 remaining to be paid. The officer assigns the 15 remaining weeks equally, starting with the first parent who applied. The first parent will be entitled to a total of 33 weeks and the other parent will be entitled to a total of 7 weeks. The officer revises the entitlement and creates an OP on both claims.

When separation monies are reviewed during that period, they are not considered earnings and are not allocated, regardless of the BPC. Do not consider separation monies that are not allocated when determining the renewal week. A transitional provision to the Budget 2021 applies to separation monies that are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362). When the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310), and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), monies paid or payable due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment are not considered earnings and are not allocated. These earnings are not considered to determine the renewal week.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the processing of claimant's reports in relation to renewal weeks and the creation of Operational Centre Memo (MM06) transactions. However, they present conflicting instructions regarding when to create the memo and how to handle claimant's reports after a renewal week. Passage 1 states that an MM06 transaction is created if there are processed or cycling reports after the renewal week, while Passage 2 states that if reports have already been processed, they should be input in CPS on the day the memo is created, indicating a different approach to handling the reports and the memo creation.
item1_text: Note Note: If benefits are payable and claimant’s reports must be processed before a renewal week, but there are processed or cycling claimant’s reports after the renewal week, the officer creates an Operational Centre Memo (MM06) transaction for an IPOC officer to process the claimant’s reports in purge and recreate (P/R) or in MPS. The officer includes information on claimant’s reports that have never been input into the system, and claimant’s reports that are cycling before the renewal week, if necessary. If there are no claimant’s reports processed or cycling after the existing renewal week, the officer inputs an earlier renewal week and the claimant’s reports in FTS.
item2_text: Note Note: Any claimant’s reports requiring input after a renewal week for which claimant’s reports have already been processed are input in CPS on the day the Operational Centre Memo (MM06) transaction is created. This leaves only the blocked weeks to be paid in P/R. If a renewal week is on the claim but no claimant’s reports have been processed from the renewal week and the renewal week should have been an earlier week, input the renewal week in the appropriate week followed by the claimant’s reports for the earlier period. If no claimant’s reports have been processed from the renewal week onward, do not create an Operational Centre Memo (MM06) transaction. Input all the claimant’s reports in CPS. Do not include any earnings, sick days, not available days or training (except for referred training) on the Operational Centre Memo (MM06) transaction.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the occurrence of an I of E in relation to an ROE and the 7-day break in work. However, they present conflicting claims regarding the conditions under which an I of E is considered to have occurred. Passage 1 states that an I of E is considered if there is at least one pay period with no earnings or if block 18 indicates a 7-day break, while Passage 2 states that an I of E has occurred only if the ROE was issued with the expectation that the client would not return within 7 days. This creates a contradiction in the criteria for determining an I of E.
item1_text: Note Note: An I of E is considered to have occurred if an ROE in the QP has at least one pay period containing no earnings or if block 18 of an ROE in the QP indicates a 7-day break in work. If information on file or on an ROE indicates that the client continues to work, fact-finding with the employer may be required. Fact-finding is not required to determine if a client returned to work before the 7-day break. If it is later learned that the employer issued the ROE knowing that the client would be called back to work within the 7-day period, the claim could be subject to cancellation, voiding or postdating (if an I of E occurred later). This is usually determined during an investigation by Integrity.
item2_text: Note Note: If an ROE was issued with the expectation that the client would not be called back to work within 7 days, an I of E has occurred. However, if the client returned to the same employment within 7 days and the claim has not been finalized, the I of E is deemed not to have taken place. The BP is not established unless an I of E has occurred at another time in the QP.

The allocation start date is between September 27, 2020 (w/c 2258) and September 24, 2021 (w/c 2309). The separation monies are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), regardless of the BPC. The separation monies are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362) and the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361). This measure applies to all EI claim types (CTs) and to EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) claims. item2_text: Note Note: A Budget 2021 measure applies to separation monies that are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361) and are paid due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment. Do not consider separation monies that are not allocated when determining the renewal week. A transitional provision to the Budget 2021 applies to separation monies that are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362). When the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310), and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), monies paid or payable due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment are not considered earnings and are not allocated.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the treatment of payments and false statements on biweekly claimant's reports for BPCs of 2063 and after. However, they contain conflicting details regarding the processing of payments and the counting of false statements. Passage 1 states that all payments will be listed as one-week payments, while Passage 2 refers to them as one-week processed payments and introduces additional complexities regarding the counting of misrepresentations and the treatment of payments. This leads to mutually incompatible claims about how payments and reports are handled.
item1_text: Note Note: For BPCs of 2063 and after, all payments will be listed as one-week payments in FTS. However, there is no change in how an officer counts false statements on biweekly claimant’s reports. One claimant’s report constitutes one count of false statements, even if the client receives 2 payments for one biweekly claimant’s report.
item2_text: Note Note: For BPCs of 2063 and after, all payments will be listed as one-week processed payments in FTS. Effective April 10, 2017, all individual payments processed by the CPS will be combined into one payment issued to the client. However, there is no change in how an officer counts misrepresentations on biweekly claimant’s reports. One claimant’s report constitutes one count of false statement, even if the client receives 2 payments for one biweekly claimant’s report or receives one payment for two or more bi-weekly claimant’s reports processed at the same time. A series of 2-week claimant’s reports are processed automatically for clients who are exempt from completing claimant’s reports. The payments are shown in FTS, but the claimant’s reports are not. When counting misrepresentations, the officer considers both paper cheques and direct deposits starting from the BPC and counting every 2-week period as one claimant’s report and one payment. If the claim ends with only a single weekly payment processed in the final week, that single week counts as one claimant’s report and one payment.

item1_text: Note Note: Separation monies are not allocated if claims meet one of the following conditions: The BPC is between March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493), and October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ). item2_text: Note Note: Pilot project no. 24 – Separation monies – w/c 2493 to w/c 2572 A temporary measure under Pilot Project No. 24 applies to separation monies paid due to a separation from employment on claims with a BPC or allocation start date between March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493) and October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ). Passage 1 states that the total weeks paid at 55% are 43 weeks with 7 weeks remaining, while Passage 2 indicates a total of 38 weeks deemed paid and mentions 12 weeks remaining. Therefore, the total weeks paid or deemed paid at 55% are 18 + 10 + 10 = 38 weeks As the claimant is on regular benefits at the time of the conversion, the benefit period will be extended by 12 weeks to allow for the remaining 12 weeks of benefits at 55%. The new LRW will be 2181 + 12 = 2193 Benefits paid: Regular 5 wks (2181 to 2185) After receiving 5 more weeks of regular benefits, the claimant requests to switch back to extended parental benefits. At week 2185, the total weeks paid or deemed paid at 55% are 18 + 10 + 10 + 5 = 43 weeks. There are 7 weeks at 55% remaining before the claimant will reach the 50 week cap. Using table 2, 7 weeks at 55% converts to 12 weeks of extended parental benefits. In order to allow the full payment of the remaining extended parental, the benefit period will have to be further extended. The current LRW on the claim is 2193. 2185 + 12 = 2197. The benefit period will have to be extended by 4 additional weeks. The new LRW will be 2193 + 4 = 2197. Benefits paid: Extended Parental 12 wks (2186 to 2197)
item2_text: Example Example: 10 weeks of regular benefits paid + 10 weeks where the client returned to work (deemed as 10 weeks paid at the basic rate) + 30 weeks of extended parental benefits = 50 weeks. CPS can no longer process payments for this client. The officer converts the 30 weeks of extended parental benefits to the equivalent of 18 weeks of standard benefits. The total number of weeks of benefits at the basic rate deemed paid to the client is therefore 10 + 10 + 18 = 38 weeks. There are 12 weeks remaining of the maximum 50 weeks allowed. The officer converts the remaining 12 weeks back to extended parental benefits to determine that the client can still receive 20 weeks of extended parental benefits.

item1_text: Note Note: The Total recoverable field on the Overpayment tab in FTS can take a few minutes to update after creating the OP in PSCD. To quickly determine the recoupment amount, the IPOC officer adds the amount of the new OP to the balance displayed in the Total recoverable field. If the amendment to the claim results in the client being paid any weeks beyond the client’s entitlement, the IPOC officer establishes an OP for the weeks in excess. The IPOC officer uses the OP message code indicated on the MM06.
item2_text: Note Note: The update of the Current recoverable and Total recoverable fields in FTS can take a few minutes to appear after creating the OP in PSCD. To quickly determine the recoupment amount, the IPOC officer adds the amount of the new OP to the balance displayed in the Current recoverable or Total recoverable fields, depending on the situation: for a misrepresentative OP, the amount is added to the Current recoverable and Total recoverable fields, because the 35-day grace period does not apply. for a non-misrepresentative OP, the amount is added only to the Total recoverable field. Once an agreed deduction shows in the Agreed deduction field or the MM06 requests the recoupment of the OP from the benefits payable, no grace period applies. The IPOC officer then adds the amount of the new OP to the balance displayed in the Current recoverable and Total recoverable fields. If the amendment to the claim results in the client being paid any weeks beyond the client’s entitlement, the IPOC officer establishes an OP for the weeks in excess. The IPOC officer uses the OP message code indicated on the MM06.

item1_text: Note Note: When a pregnancy is terminated within the first 19 weeks, the claim is treated as a sickness claim. If a pregnancy is terminated after the 19th week, the claim is treated as a maternity claim and the DOB is used to determine the maternity window. To calculate which week is the 19th week, the officer uses the following formula: [w/c of the expected DOB] – 39 + 18 Example: The expected DOB is December 16, 2020 (w/c 2269), but the client’s pregnancy is terminated on August 29, 2020 (w/c 2253). 19th week calculation: w/c 2269 – 39 + 18 = w/c 2248 Since w/c 2253 is after the 19th week, the claim is treated as a maternity claim and the w/c 2253 is coded as the actual DOB.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the processing of payments and the counting of misrepresentations related to claimant's reports. However, they present conflicting information regarding how payments are counted and reported. Passage 1 states that one claimant's report constitutes one count of false statement regardless of the number of payments, while Passage 2 indicates that each pair of payments is counted as one payment and one false statement based on one claimant's report. This creates a contradiction in how misrepresentations are counted.
item1_text: Note Note: For BPCs of 2063 and after, all payments will be listed as one-week processed payments in FTS. Effective April 10, 2017, all individual payments processed by the CPS will be combined into one payment issued to the client. However, there is no change in how an officer counts misrepresentations on biweekly claimant’s reports. One claimant’s report constitutes one count of false statement, even if the client receives 2 payments for one biweekly claimant’s report or receives one payment for two or more bi-weekly claimant’s reports processed at the same time. A series of 2-week claimant’s reports are processed automatically for clients who are exempt from completing claimant’s reports. The payments are shown in FTS, but the claimant’s reports are not. When counting misrepresentations, the officer considers both paper cheques and direct deposits starting from the BPC and counting every 2-week period as one claimant’s report and one payment. If the claim ends with only a single weekly payment processed in the final week, that single week counts as one claimant’s report and one payment.
item2_text: Note Note: For BPCs of w/c 2063 and after, all payments will be listed as one-week payments in FTS, even though the claimant’s reports are processed biweekly. Therefore, officers count each pair of payments listed as one payment and one false statement based on one claimant’s report.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss the process and implications of changing parental benefits, emphasizing the importance of the most recent request by the first parent and the need for correction if the incorrect type is paid.
