item1_text: Info Example: While receiving maternity benefits, the first parent who applied requests to change the type of parental benefits from standard to extended. The other parent then applies for and receives extended parental benefits for the same child. Due to processing delays, the change request made by the first parent is not actioned. When the claim is automatically converted from maternity to parental benefits, the first parent receives standard parental benefits as originally requested. The first parent’s claim must be corrected to extended parental benefits because this was the most recent type of parental benefits that the parent to apply first selected, before parental benefits were paid. When the officer contacts the first parent to discuss the impact of the change on the claim, the first parent requests to cancel the change to extended parental benefits. The officer advises the first parent that the type of parental benefits selected becomes irrevocable once parental benefits have been paid.
item2_text: Info Note: When a request to change the type of parental benefits is not actioned immediately and the incorrect type of parental benefits is paid, the claim must be corrected. item1_text: Callout Hello, We are writing to you about your Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB). When you first applied for the CERB through Service Canada, you received a payment of $2,000. This was an advance of four weeks of the CERB, which was issued in order to get money in your pocket as quickly as possible. You previously received an email about the recovery of the first half ($1,000) of the advance payment, which explained that your CERB payments would be impacted at that time. We are now writing to you about the second half of the advance. Depending on your reporting schedule and ongoing need for benefits, to recover the remaining $1,000 of the advance payment, you will receive either no payment when you complete your next report or two reduced payments (i.e. of $500) when you complete your next two reports. Your payments will resume as long as you continue reporting. There will be no further gaps in your CERB payments. Please continue completing reports to show that you are eligible for all weeks of the CERB, including the four weeks of the benefit covered by the advance payment. The CERB is taxable, which means we will provide you with a tax slip so you can report any payments you received on your 2020 income tax return. As we begin to restart the economy and get people back on the job, Canadians receiving the CERB should be actively seeking work opportunities or planning to return to work, provided they are able and it is reasonable to do so. Jobbank.gc.ca, Canada’s national employment service, offers a free online database of job listings in Canada, as well as other employment services and information for job seekers, including career planning, resume creation, job matching and alerts. If you continue to need financial assistance after the CERB ends, you may be eligible for Employment Insurance and we will communicate with you in the coming weeks with more details. Sincerely,
item2_text: Callout Hello, We are writing to you about your Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB). In spring 2020, you received an initial CERB payment of $2,000. The maximum amount you should have received is $500 per week during the full period you were eligible for the CERB. According to information we have on file, including your reporting information, you were paid more benefits than the amount for which you were eligible. The Notice of Debt provides details on what you owe and instructions on how to make payment arrangements, if necessary. If you have additional information to provide that could modify our decision and impact the amount you owe: contact Service Canada: English: 1-800-206-7218, French: 1-800-808-6352, TTY: 1-800-529-3742; or complete a service request at canada.ca/service-canada-e-service. You have 30 days following the date of the Notice of Debt to make a formal request for reconsideration if you disagree with this decision. For more information, and to access the Request for Reconsideration of an Employment Insurance decision form, visit ei.gc.ca or contact Service Canada using the information above. Sincerely, Canada Employment Insurance Commission

item2_text: Example 1 Example 1: Three consecutive weeks of casual sickness benefits have been paid in the BP. w/c 2386 (March 12, 2023) = BPC; w/c 2387 to w/c 2393 (March 19 to May 6, 2023) = 7 weeks of regular benefits; w/c 2394-1 — the client becomes ill; w/c 2394 to w/c 2396 (May 7 to 27, 2023) = 3 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid on a claim for regular benefits (CT 2); w/c 2397 (May 28, 2023) conversion to sickness benefits requested. item2_text: Note Note: A Budget 2021 measure applies to separation monies that are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361) and are paid due to a permanent separation from employment. item1_text: Callout Hello, We are writing to you about your Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB). When you first applied for the CERB through Service Canada, you received a payment of $2,000. This was an advance of four weeks of the CERB, which was issued in order to get money in your pocket as quickly as possible. You previously received an email about the recovery of the first half ($1,000) of the advance payment, which explained that your CERB payments would be impacted at that time. We are now writing to you about the second half of the advance. Depending on your reporting schedule and ongoing need for benefits, to recover the remaining $1,000 of the advance payment, you will receive either no payment when you complete your next report or two reduced payments (i.e. of $500) when you complete your next two reports. Your payments will resume as long as you continue reporting. There will be no further gaps in your CERB payments. Please continue completing reports to show that you are eligible for all weeks of the CERB, including the four weeks of the benefit covered by the advance payment. The CERB is taxable, which means we will provide you with a tax slip so you can report any payments you received on your 2020 income tax return. As we begin to restart the economy and get people back on the job, Canadians receiving the CERB should be actively seeking work opportunities or planning to return to work, provided they are able and it is reasonable to do so. Jobbank.gc.ca, Canada’s national employment service, offers a free online database of job listings in Canada, as well as other employment services and information for job seekers, including career planning, resume creation, job matching and alerts. If you continue to need financial assistance after the CERB ends, you may be eligible for Employment Insurance and we will communicate with you in the coming weeks with more details. Sincerely,
item2_text: Callout “We are writing to inform you about the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) paid to you through Service Canada under the Employment Insurance Act. Section 153.9 (4) of the Employment Insurance Act stipulates that in order to be eligible to CERB, your income cannot exceed $1000 over a four-week period for which CERB was paid to you. These weeks succeed each other in chronological order but not necessarily consecutively. You have earned more that $1000 over one or more four-week period(s) in which CERB was paid to you. For this reason, you are not eligible to the CERB you received for the following period(s): From [disentitlement start date] to [disentitlement end date] [The following is optional if more than one period:] and from [disentitlement start date] to [disentitlement end date].” If the client made a repayment , type: “As a result of this decision, we have created an overpayment on your claim and the amount of $[amount] you repaid to Service Canada will be applied to this overpayment [, resulting in no outstanding debt]. If you repaid your CERB in 2020 or 2021, an amended T4E will be issued to you to reflect the repayment. The amended T4E could also have an impact on your income tax return. For more information, including how to request a change to your tax return, visit canada.ca/change-tax-return . canada.ca/change-tax-return For any questions on your T4E, visit canada.ca/ei and consult Employment Insurance Tax Slips (T4Es) .” If the client has an outstanding debt , type: “You will soon receive a Notice of Debt with the details on what you owe and instructions on how to make payment arrangements. item2_text: Example 2 Example 2: A client files a claim and requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits. The other parent subsequently requests 35 weeks of standard parental benefits, but the first parent has already received 3 weeks. Since there are only 37 remaining weeks of benefits and the parents cannot decide how to share the benefits, a decision is made for them. The number of remaining weeks cannot be equally divided between them. The remaining weeks are divided as equally as possible and the extra week is assigned to the parent who first applied for parental benefits. item1_text: Info Example: For a contract period of September 1, 2000 to August 31, 2001 with a salary of $35,000, the daily average earnings are calculated as follows: Total number of calendar days within the contract period = 365 days Daily average earnings = $35,000 ÷ 365 = $96 The total insurable earnings to be reported on the ROE is the daily average earnings multiplied by 189 days: ($96 × 189 days = $18,144)
item2_text: Example (a teacher) Example (a teacher): First contract was from September 1, 1999 to August 31, 2000 with a salary of $30,000. Second contract is from September 1, 2000 to August 31. 2001 with a salary of $35,000. Teacher has an interruption of earnings on November 3, 2000. Number of calendar days in 1 st contract = 366 Average daily earnings = $30,000 ÷ 365 = $82 Number of calendar days in 2 nd contract = 365 Average daily earnings = $35,000 ÷ 365 = $96 Number of calendar days in 2 nd contract Counting back from the last day worked: November 3, 2000 - September 1, 2000 = 64 days Total insurable earnings: 64 × $96 $ = $6,144 Number of calendar days to report from the 1 st contract: 189 days - 64 days = 125 days (August 31, 2000 back to April 29, 2000) Total insurable earnings: 125 × $82 = $10,250 The total insurable earnings to be reported on the ROE are the insurable earnings obtained from the 2 nd contract added to the insurable earnings obtained from the 1 st contract: ($10,250 + $6,144 = $16,394)

item1_text: Note Note: For claims with a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, 420 hours of insurable employment is required to establish a claim for regular or special benefits, regardless of the conversion date. If the client has 420 or more insurable hours, select the major attached option.

However, if the client initially requested regular benefits, the claim cannot be converted to special benefits on a conversion request.

item2_text: Example 1 Example 1: Three consecutive weeks of casual sickness benefits have been paid in the BP. w/c 2386 (March 12, 2023) = BPC; w/c 2387 to w/c 2393 (March 19 to May 6, 2023) = 7 weeks of regular benefits; w/c 2394-1 — the client becomes ill; w/c 2394 to w/c 2396 (May 7 to 27, 2023) = 3 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid on a claim for regular benefits (CT 2); w/c 2397 (May 28, 2023) = conversion to sickness benefits requested. The officer considers the 3 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid in the BP when determining the recovery week. Recovery week: [conversion week (w/c 2397)] + [8 weeks (w/c 2405)] – [3 weeks of casual sickness paid in the BP] = [recovery week w/c 2402 (July 8, 2023)] If all of the relevant conversion conditions are met, the officer establishes the recovery week as w/c 2402. Example 2: There are 2 separate periods of casual sickness benefits totaling 6 weeks paid in the BP: w/c 2386 (March 12, 2023) = BPC; w/c 2387 to w/c 2393 (March 19 to May 6, 2023) = 7 weeks of regular benefits; w/c 2394-1 — the client becomes ill; w/c 2394 to w/c 2395 (May 7 to 20, 2023) = 2 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid on a claim for regular benefits (CT 2); w/c 2396 to w/c 2405 (May 21 to July 29, 2023) = 10 weeks of regular benefits; w/c 2406-1 — the client becomes ill again; w/c 2406 to w/c 2409 (July 30 to August 26, 2023) = 4 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid on a claim for regular benefits (CT 2); a total of 6 weeks of casual sickness has been paid in the BP; the client has not recovered and is requesting sickness benefits after w/c 2409; w/c 2410 (August 27, 2023) = conversion to sickness benefits required as 4 consecutive weeks of casual sickness have been paid and the client has not recovered. The officer considers all 6 weeks of casual sickness benefits paid in the BP when determining the recovery week. Recovery week: [conversion week (w/c 2410)] + [8 weeks (w/c 2418)] – [6 weeks of casual sickness paid in the BP] = [recovery week w/c 2412 (September 16, 2023)]. If all of the relevant conversion conditions are met, the officer establishes the recovery week as w/c 2412. item2_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend the funeral of an immediate family member. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will not be returning to Canada until May 20, 2016. To determine the 7-day allowable period, the officer must exclude the day of departure (May 9, 2016) and count 7 consecutive days beginning with May 10, 2016. The 7-day allowable period will end as of May 16, 2016. A D59 is imposed from May 9, 2016 (the day of departure) to May 16, 2016 (the allowable period of 7 days following the day of departure). Since the client is not returning to Canada until a later date, a D13 is imposed effective May 17, 2016 up to and including May 19, 2016, the day before the return date.

final_analysis: Both passages discuss measures from Budget 2021, but they provide conflicting details regarding the treatment of earnings and separation monies during the specified periods. Passage 1 states that a minimum amount of SE earnings is required to qualify, while Passage 2 indicates that separation monies are not considered earnings and are not allocated during the same timeframe, leading to mutually incompatible claims.
item1_text: Note Note: As part of Budget 2021, a temporary measure sets the minimum amount of SE earnings required to qualify to $5,289. This applies to claims with a BPC between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 18, 2022 (w/c 2361).
item2_text: Note Note: A Budget 2021 measure applies to separation monies that are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), and are paid due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment. When separation monies are reviewed during that period, they are not considered earnings and are not allocated, regardless of the BPC. A transitional provision to the Budget 2021 applies to separation monies that are reviewed on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362). When the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), monies paid or payable due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment are not considered earnings and are not allocated.

item2_text: Example 1 Example 1: A client leaves Canada on May 9, 2016 to attend the funeral of an immediate family member. The client is allowed 7 consecutive days to be out of Canada for this purpose. The client will not be returning to Canada until May 20, 2016. To determine the 7-day allowable period, the officer must exclude the day of departure (May 9, 2016) and count 7 consecutive days beginning with May 10, 2016. The 7-day allowable period will end as of May 16, 2016. A D59 is imposed from May 9, 2016 (the day of departure) to May 16, 2016 (the allowable period of 7 days following the day of departure). Since the client is not returning to Canada until a later date, a D13 is imposed effective May 17, 2016 up to and including May 19, 2016, the day before the return date.

item1_text: Note Note: For initial and recalculation claims with a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, any contentious RFS in the QP that is not the last period of employment does not require adjudication. All ROEs are included in the calculation. This measure does not apply to claims for SE or fishing benefits.
item2_text: Note Note: If the BPC is between w/c 2258 and w/c 2309, calculate the 12-week period before the most recent I of E. When answering question 5, consider any contentious RFS issues that occurred before the 12-week period as not being in the QP. On claims with a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, adjudication is only required on the last RFS. Even if there are other contentious ROEs in the QP, the officer can defer adjudication on the client’s most recent I of E. Therefore, adjudication deferral before a disqualifying event no longer applies. This measure does not apply on claims for SE or fishing benefits. For all claims with a tentative BPC of w/c 2361, ADJ WIs are created for the last period of employment and for any other contentious periods of employment in the QP. Officers follow normal procedures to adjudicate those WIs because the final BPC can be w/c 2362 or later. However, if the final BPC is between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, the system applies the Budget 2021 temporary measures.
